summary.text: Group theory studies groups, algebraic structures that are central to abstract algebra.
Rings, fields and vector spaces can all be seen as groups with additional operations and axioms.
Symmetry groups model crystals, the hydrogen atom and three of the four known fundamental forces, and group theory is also central to public key cryptography.

paragraphs.heading: What group theory studies
paragraphs.text: Group theory is the part of abstract algebra that studies structures called groups. The idea of a group sits at the center of abstract algebra. Rings, fields and vector spaces, which are other well-known structures, can each be viewed as a group with extra operations and rules added on top. Groups turn up again and again across mathematics, and the methods of group theory have shaped many parts of algebra.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters outside mathematics
paragraphs.text: Symmetry groups can model physical systems such as crystals and the hydrogen atom. Three of the universe's four known fundamental forces can be modelled this way too. For this reason group theory, together with the closely linked representation theory, has many uses in physics, chemistry and materials science. Group theory is also central to public key cryptography.

paragraphs.heading: Where the idea came from
paragraphs.text: The early history of groups goes back to the 19th century. Lagrange, Ruffini and Abel found early results about permutation groups while hunting for general ways to solve polynomial equations of high degree. Évariste Galois coined the word "group" and tied groups to field theory, a link now known as Galois theory. In the 1830s Galois was the first to use groups to decide whether polynomial equations can be solved. Cayley and Cauchy then went further and created the theory of permutation groups.

paragraphs.heading: Several roots, one theory
paragraphs.text: Within geometry, groups first gained importance in projective geometry, and after that in non-Euclidean geometry. Felix Klein's Erlangen program declared group theory to be the organizing principle of geometry. In 1884 Sophus Lie began attaching groups, now called Lie groups, to problems in analysis. The theory was unified starting around 1880. Since then its influence has kept growing, and it gave rise to abstract algebra itself in the early 20th century.

paragraphs.heading: Permutation groups
paragraphs.text: Permutation groups were the first class of groups to be studied in a systematic way. Take any set X and a collection G of permutations, which are bijections of X into itself. If G contains the composite and the inverse of each of its members, then G forms a group that acts on X. When X has n elements and G holds every permutation, G is the symmetric group Sₙ. Cayley showed early on that any group can be pictured as a permutation group acting on itself.

paragraphs.heading: Matrix groups
paragraphs.text: The next important class is matrix groups, also called linear groups. Here G is a set of invertible matrices of a fixed order n over a field K, and G is closed under products and inverses. Each such group acts by linear transformations on Kⁿ, the vector space of dimension n. Permutation groups and matrix groups are both special cases of transformation groups, which act on a space while keeping its structure intact. For permutation groups that space is a set; for matrix groups it is a vector space.

paragraphs.heading: A striking consequence
paragraphs.text: Often the structure of a permutation group can be studied through the way it acts on its set. Used this way, the approach shows the alternating group Aₙ to be simple whenever n ≥ 5, meaning it has no proper normal subgroups. That fact plays a key part in showing a general algebraic equation of degree n ≥ 5 cannot be solved in radicals. One of the most important feats of 20th-century mathematics was a joint effort that ended in a complete classification of finite simple groups. It filled more than 10,000 journal pages, mostly published between 1960 and 2004.
